summary:
Exoplanet Explorer is a free web app that helps students explore planets beyond our solar system, even without a telescope. Using data from the NASA Exoplanet Archive, it shows 25 well-known confirmed exoplanets on an interactive map of distance from Earth and length of year. Students can search and filter planets, compare each one with Earth, and calculate how old they would be there. A “Learn the basics” section explains in simple language how planets are found, what the habitable zone is, and what the units mean. Students can also add their own sky photos and drawings to each planet.

The app turns complex NASA data into something clear and hands-on for school students, including those with little access to telescopes or science resources. It matters because it builds curiosity and science skills early. In future, local users could upload their own telescope observations to grow a shared community map of the night sky.
details:
What it does: Exoplanet Explorer is a free web app that lets students explore planets outside our solar system. It shows 25 well-known confirmed exoplanets on an interactive map of distance from Earth against the length of a planet’s year. Students can search, filter by discovery method or habitable zone, and sort the list. Each planet has a detail view that compares its size with Earth, shows its distance, mass and discovery year, and calculates how old the student would be on that planet. A “Learn the basics” section explains in simple language what an exoplanet is, how planets are found, what the habitable zone means, and what the units mean.

Benefits and impact: Many students have no telescope and find NASA’s data hard to read. The app turns real NASA data into something clear and hands-on that works on any phone or computer with no login or install. Our goal is to build curiosity about space science in school students.

Data and tools: We used the NASA Exoplanet Archive as our NASA data source. The app is built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and SVG, and uses the Sora font. AI (Claude) helped us build the app and write text. The planet pictures are simple illustrations drawn with code, not real photos, and they are labelled as illustrations.

Creativity: We made space data personal with the “your age on this planet” calculator, and we let students add their own sky photos and drawings to each planet. The map shows hundreds of light-years of space in one simple view.

Factors we considered: Accessibility for beginners, clear explanations, honest labelling of illustrations versus real data, and student privacy (added photos stay on the student’s own device). The app currently uses a snapshot of well-known planets with rounded values. In future we plan to connect it to the full live archive, let local users upload telescope observations, and add a shared photo gallery.
